title: Symmetry Properties of Bound States in the Continuum in Hexagonal Lattice Photonic Crystal Slabs
abstract: Bound states in the continuum (BICs) within photonic crystal (PhC) cavities realise the full confinement of light despite lying within the continuum of radiation modes. While their diverse practical applications has attracted considerable research interest, developing the fundamental understanding of BICs is important for the design of future devices. This paper uses a group theoretical approach to determine the basis functions of the irreducible representations (irreps) of a PhC with the symmetry of the $C_{6v}$ space group, from which the spatial distribution of the electromagnetic fields within the cavity can be determined. Furthermore, the reflection parity of the electric field and a $k \cdot p$ perturbation theory approach are used to determine the far-field polarisation of each irrep. The $k \cdot p$ perturbation explains why the $E_2$ irrep has a topological charge of $-2$, as well as showing that a topological charge does not necessarily indicate the presence of a BIC. Additionally, it is found that the quality factor of the modes do not necessarily scale as $Q \propto 1/|k|^{2|q|}$, but are instead dependent on the coupling to the radiative mode in the $k \cdot p$ perturbation, which is determined from the symmetry of each irrep.
summary: This paper investigates the symmetry properties of Bound States in the Continuum (BICs) in hexagonal photonic crystal slabs using group theory. By analyzing the system's irreducible representations and applying $k \cdot p$ theory, the authors determine that the confinement quality factor and topological charge are fundamentally governed by the underlying crystal symmetry. This provides a powerful theoretical framework for designing next-generation photonic devices.
main_problem: The paper aims to develop a fundamental understanding of Bound States in the Continuum (BICs) within photonic crystal (PhC) cavities by analyzing their symmetry properties.
main_result: The analysis uses group theory and $k \cdot p$ perturbation theory to characterize BICs, showing that their quality factor scaling and topological charge are dictated by the irreducible representation symmetry of the lattice.
method: The study employs a group theoretical approach based on the $C_{6v}$ space group symmetry, combined with $k \cdot p$ perturbation theory and the calculation of far-field polarization via Stokes parameters.
model_or_system: The physical system is a photonic crystal slab with a hexagonal lattice structure. The analysis determines the basis functions for the irreducible representations (irreps) of this system.
key_observables: Quality factor ($Q$), Topological Charge ($T_C$ or $q$), Far-field polarization angle ($\psi(\mathbf{k}_{\|})$), and the symmetry-derived basis functions.
important_parameters: The $C_{6v}$ point group symmetry, the wave vector $\mathbf{k}$ near the $\Gamma$ point, and the coupling strength to the radiative mode.
main_assumptions: The analysis focuses on the TE mode polarization and utilizes the $k \cdot p$ theory near the $\Gamma$ point for far-field analysis.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the symmetry properties in real and reciprocal space, the band structure, and the method for calculating far-field polarization distributions for various modes.
paper_structure: The paper proceeds by first establishing the symmetry framework using group theory to find basis functions for the $C_{6v}$ irreps. It then applies $k \cdot p$ theory and reflection parity to determine far-field polarization and topological charges, concluding with an analysis of how the $Q$ factor depends on the irrep symmetry.
why_interesting: The rigorous application of group theory to photonic band structure analysis provides powerful tools for predicting and understanding mode confinement, which is crucial for designing high-quality optical cavities relevant to quantum optics and photonics.

figures.caption: FIG. 1: (a) and (b) The symmetries of a PhC belonging to the C6v group in real and reciprocal space respectively. High symmetry points and lines in reciprocal space are shown. (c) Band structure of the same PhC calculated using the finite-element method (FEM) method in COMSOL Multiphysics. Simulation details are provided in Section IV. (d) Illustrative diagram explaining the method for calculating the far-field polarisation. (e) Far-field polarisation distributions for different topological charges (TCs).

FIG. 2: Electromagnetic fields within a unit cell for each of the 6 irreps with n = 0. Colour plot shows the imaginary part of the magnetic field. Arrows represent the real part of the electric field. While any linear combination of Ei(1) and Ei(2) for i = 1, 2 are an acceptable basis function, the angular momentum basis vectors (x, y) and (x2 −y2, −2xy) have been chosen as the basis functions for convenience.

FIG. 3: The four possible methods by which the parity can decompose. Solid lines represent the far-field polarisation, while dotted lines represent the high symmetry lines with odd parity. (a) and (b) possess a TC of 1, while (c) and (d) possess a TC of -2.

FIG. 4: Near-field distribution of the unit cell in the six bound resonance / BIC modes at the Γ point. The colour plot shows the distribution of the imaginary component of the magnetic field, while the arrows represent the direction of the electric field.
